cards.title: Optimal input-sparsity subspace embeddings
cards.formal: Is the optimal-dimension sparse oblivious subspace-embedding conjecture true? Precisely, does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that for every pair of integers \(n\ge d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\), there are an integer \(m\) and a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) over real \(m\times n\) matrices with \[1\le m\le\left\lceil C\,\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil,\qquad s=\left\lceil C\,\frac{\log(d/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\] such that every matrix in the support has at most \(s\) nonzero entries per column and, for every \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pr_{\Pi\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\ \forall x\in W:\ (1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|\Pi x\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\ \bigr]\ge1-\delta?\] The row and column-sparsity bounds must hold simultaneously, with no additional growing factors.
cards.why: Subspace embeddings compress a matrix’s column space while preserving the lengths of all its linear combinations. Small output dimension reduces later computation, and sparse embedding columns reduce the arithmetic needed to apply the map to sparse data. The conjecture asks whether these two advantages can be attained together at the stated dependence on accuracy and failure probability.
cards.status_note: The checked ICALP 2025 and SODA 2026 sources retain the exact dimension/sparsity conjecture. The SODA improvement has sub-polylogarithmic losses and stated parameter restrictions, so it does not settle the all-parameter target here. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-15 found no exact resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-status certification.

cards.definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.

The preserved norm guarantee concerns one entire fixed subspace. An embedding for selected vectors alone or one constructed using the particular matrix is a different object from an oblivious subspace embedding.

cards.definitions: The input gives \(n\ge 0, V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), and two symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is \(H=(V,E_{1}\cap E_{2})\), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points \(p(v)\in \mathbb{R} ^{2}\) to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints \(p(u),p(v)\), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same \(p(v)\) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in \(E_{1}\cap E_{2}\). Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) with at most \(C(N+1)^{c}\) bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

context_blocks.title: Two compatible views of the same objects
context_blocks.text: Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

context_blocks.title: The union need not be planar
context_blocks.text: Take \(G_{1}\) to be \(K_{5}\) with one edge deleted and \(G_{2}\) to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. \(G_{1}\) is planar, and \(G_{2}\) can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to \(G_{1}\). This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph \(K_{5}\). Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

context_blocks.title: The connected common case is solved
context_blocks.text: The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

context_blocks.title: Which nearby results apply
context_blocks.text: Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.

cards.title: Euclidean minimum spanning tree complexity
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(d\geq3\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic worst-case time for computing an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of \(n\geq2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\). The input is the array of coordinates of the points \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\); the output is a list of \(n-1\) pairs of indices forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) that minimizes \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\) over all spanning trees on these labels. Include logarithmic factors in the requested complexity, and use the real-arithmetic model below.
cards.why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.

cards.definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n)\) for every fixed \(d\geq3\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of matching uniform upper and lower bounds. For each \(d\), one correct deterministic program must have worst-case time at most \(C_dg_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Every correct program must have worst-case time at least \(c_{A,d}g_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(c_{A,d}>0\). The constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\) and, for the lower bound, on the program. An approximation scheme, an expected-time bound alone, or the polynomial exponent without matching logarithmic factors does not determine this target.

context_blocks.text: The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. This card makes its resource question concrete by requesting optimal deterministic arithmetic complexity in every fixed dimension at least three. This is an editorial sharpening of the source’s informal word “close,” not an assertion that the source prescribed a particular logarithmic overhead.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.

cards.title: Exact planar Euclidean matching
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors including logarithmic factors, the optimal deterministic worst-case running time for computing a minimum-length perfect matching of \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for all integers \(n\geq1\), in the exact real-arithmetic model below. The output is a list of \(n\) unordered pairs of input indices, every index occurring exactly once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\) among all perfect matchings. The input consists only of the point coordinates; the complete graph is implicit.
cards.why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.

cards.definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(g:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds in the stated model. The upper bound must give one uniform deterministic algorithm with worst-case time at most \(C g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The lower bound must show that every correct uniform algorithm has worst-case time at least \(c_A g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), where \(c_A>0\) and the threshold may depend on the algorithm. Constants are independent of the point configuration and \(n\). Approximate matchings, a bound only for bipartite matching, or a polynomial exponent with unresolved logarithmic factors do not meet this criterion.

cards.title: NP certificates for homeomorphism of three-manifolds
cards.formal: Does homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds, have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) of total encoded length \(N\), \[H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;V(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the NP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem below.
cards.why: Short certificates would separate the cost of discovering topological equivalence from the cost of checking it. An NP upper bound would place a fundamental classification problem within the standard theory of efficient verification.
cards.status_note: The NP question is explicit in the 2024 report and Jackson’s 2024/2025 article. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no general certificate theorem. cards.definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed existence of \(p,V\) with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer needs completeness for every homeomorphic promised pair and soundness against every candidate witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair, with polynomial worst-case verification time in \(N+|w|\). The verifier need not find the witness. A negative answer must exclude all polynomially bounded certificate systems in this model, not merely certificates made from a particular type of topological transformation. A result restricted to a fixed manifold, orientable closed manifolds, or one geometric class does not settle the full domain.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s Question 3 asks whether Homeo(3) lies in NP. His standing domain is compact connected manifolds supplied by triangulations. The boundary, orientation and binary-verifier conventions above make that domain explicit.

Two very different tetrahedron lists can describe the same space. A positive certificate must establish equality of the represented topological types, rather than just exhibit a relabelling of the supplied pieces. Its form is unrestricted; the polynomial bound concerns the entire witness and its verification.

Kuperberg proves an elementary-recursive decision algorithm for closed oriented 3-manifolds: the running time has a fixed-height exponential-tower bound. This establishes a quantitative decidability result in that setting, not polynomial certificates for the broader domain.

Jackson proves NP recognition for compact orientable Seifert fibered spaces with nonempty boundary, together with NP and coNP certification for their naming problem. The paper explicitly asks about general homeomorphism, which its special-class results do not decide.

NP verification concerns yes instances. It does not imply a polynomial-time method for constructing a homeomorphism, nor provide short certificates when the manifolds differ. The latter is the separate coNP question.

The 2025 seminar report asks a related fixed-parameter tractability question measured by the treewidth of the input triangulations. A parameter-dependent algorithm with no global polynomial bound would not by itself resolve this certificate question.

cards.definitions: The input lists \(n\ge 0\) distinct points \((x_{i},y_{i})\), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight \(\mathrm{W}(T)=\sum _{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\sqrt{(x_{i}- x_{j})^{2}+(y_{i}- y_{j})^{2}}\). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality \(\mathrm{W}(T)=B\) is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if \(V(x,y)\) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.

context_blocks.title: The geometry is small; the lengths need not be rational
context_blocks.text: A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. cards.definitions: General position means every subset of at most \(d+1\) input points is affinely independent. The convex hull is \(H=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Its proper nonempty faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes; a facet has dimension \(d-1\). The promise makes \(H\) full-dimensional and simplicial, with exactly \(d\) vertices per facet. Output each proper nonempty face by its set of input-vertex indices and list every containment incidence between faces of consecutive dimensions; also identify the facets. The total output size is \(O_d(f)\). Interior input points need not be output. Let \(\mathcal D_d\) be the pairs \((n,f)\) realized by a valid input, and let \(T_A(n,f)\) be the supremum of algorithm \(A\)’s steps over all such inputs with exactly these parameters. One finite deterministic program per fixed \(d\) must work for all \(n\); it is given neither \(f\) nor advice. The model has exact real registers with rational program constants and indexed memory; \(+,-,\times,/\), comparisons, copies and memory accesses cost one each. Integer indices and counters have \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits at time \(t\), with ordinary word arithmetic and comparisons charged. No floor, extraction of real digits, or free geometric query is available. Reading input and reporting faces are charged. cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the minimum sketch length \(s(n,c)\) for approximating planar earth mover distance for every integer \(n\geq2\) and real approximation factor \(c\geq1\). cards.definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_1=|x-u|+|y-v|\); grid spacing and point mass are both one. Empty sets are allowed and their distance is zero. There are no repeated points, arbitrary real weights or bounds on cardinality beyond \(|A|=|B|\leq n^2\). A length-\(s\) scheme for parameters \((n,c)\) is a probability space of public seeds \(R\), encoders \(L_R:2^{[n]^2}\to\{0,1\}^s\), and decoders \(D_R:\{0,1\}^s\times\{0,1\}^s\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\), with all relevant events measurable. The estimate is \(D_R(L_R(A),L_R(B))\). The seed is independent of the inputs and available to both encoders and the decoder. Seed length and local computation are unrestricted and not charged; this is information-theoretic sketch length in bits, not streaming update time or the dimension of a real vector. The decoder knows \(n,c,R\), but receives no input-dependent information beyond the two sketches; any stored cardinality is charged. The same encoder works for both inputs. Success is required for each fixed pair chosen independently of \(R\), not simultaneously for all pairs under one seed or against adaptive exposure of the seed. When \(A=B\), success requires estimate zero. Define \(s(n,c)\) as the least integer \(s\geq0\) admitting such a scheme; it is finite because the entire \(n^2\)-bit incidence vector can be stored. The displayed interval fixes the usual one-sided multiplicative convention explicitly; it is not an additive-error guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g(n,c)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \(a g(n,c)\leq s(n,c)\leq b g(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\) and every \(c\geq1\). The upper bound must supply schemes with the stated probability and bit length; the lower bound must cover all allowed, possibly nonlinear, public-coin schemes. Constants and \(n_0\) cannot depend on \(c\), so varying approximation regimes and logarithmic factors must be accounted for. A single upper bound, a linear-embedding lower bound alone, or the answer for only one fixed approximation factor does not determine the requested tradeoff.

context_blocks.text: Indyk’s 2011 question asks for the sketch-length/approximation tradeoff and highlights the possibility of constant \(c\) with \(s=\operatorname{polylog}n\). The card retains that full tradeoff and specifies the grid, masses, randomness and approximation convention.

A sketch must be computed without seeing the other set. The decoder then estimates one transport cost from two compressed descriptions. A fast algorithm that reads both complete inputs can exploit information that the sketch decoder does not have.

Andoni, Do Ba, Indyk and Woodruff prove that, for any fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), a sketch of polynomially sublinear grid-size dependence can obtain approximation \(O(1/\varepsilon)\). Their Theorem 1.1 uses \(O(n^\varepsilon)\) integer coordinates of polynomial magnitude; for sets this converts to \(O(n^\varepsilon\log n)\) bits. Thus constant-factor approximation is possible with more than polylogarithmic space in the stated construction.

Andoni, Krauthgamer and Razenshteyn prove that the full planar transportation norm cannot have both constant approximation and constant-size distance-threshold sketches. That norm allows general signed real mass vectors; the theorem neither identifies this subset-only bit tradeoff nor rules out polylogarithmic sketches.

The published STOC 2026 lower bound of Gartland and Ostrovskii closes the planar \(L_1\)-distortion gap for transportation cost spaces at order \(\log n\). An embedding theorem is not a theorem about every arbitrary decoder of two finite sketches, so this result does not automatically resolve the present question.

The number of grid locations and the number of occupied points are different parameters. Here the grid side length is the parameter and every equal-size pair is covered. Likewise, replacing the one-unit point masses by arbitrary weighted distributions would enlarge the input family.

cards.definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.

context_blocks.text: At each point of space, the nearest-line set describes which sites compete to be closest. Regions with one nearest line, interfaces with two, curves with three, and isolated points with four form the strata counted here. A stratum can have several connected components, and unbounded components count as well. Counting just the input lines would omit this geometric arrangement.

The question concerns Euclidean distance to complete affine lines in three dimensions. The source records a quadratic lower bound and an upper bound of \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), leaving a full exponent gap. A nearest-point diagram, a planar diagram, or a polyhedral distance function is a different object.

The conjectured guarantee is \(n^{2+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with a constant allowed to depend on that exponent slack. It does not require a single \(Cn^2\) bound. Conversely, a bound with one fixed exponent strictly above two does not meet the universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).

The source also distinguishes the full diagram from a fixed-distance level set, describable through a union of cylinders. Complexity controlled at one distance does not automatically count all strata of the nearest-site partition throughout space.

The March 2026 four-line classification describes a base case with zero through eight Voronoi vertices under general-position assumptions. The result clarifies local configurations, but fixes the number of sites and supplies no asymptotic bound for arbitrary input size.

The August 2026 regulus preprint claims quadratic total complexity when all lines lie in one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric: one of the two line families covering that surface. Its hypotheses strongly restrict the line configuration. It explicitly retains the broader quadratic-to-cubic gap for arbitrary Euclidean line sites. The present card spells out its own regular-stratum convention rather than leaving “general position” undefined.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.

cards.formal: Does nonhomeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Allow boundary and nonorientable manifolds. cards.definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(p,W\) exist, or that none exist. A positive answer needs a short accepted witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair and rejection of every candidate witness for every homeomorphic promised pair. Verification time must be polynomial in \(N+|w|\) on every binary input. A particular invariant that distinguishes only some pairs is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out all polynomial certificate systems, rather than showing the inadequacy of one invariant or representation. cards.definitions: The input includes a bounded axis-aligned box \(B\) with nonempty interior, real coordinates of vertices, an embedded finite triangle mesh containing \(\partial B\), and the labels of the two incident regions of every triangle (one label is the exterior on \(\partial B\)). Nondegenerate closed triangles meet only in a common whole edge, a common vertex, or not at all. The input is promised to describe the boundaries of a partition: bounded regions are closures of the connected components of \(\operatorname{int}(B)\) minus the mesh, with disjoint interiors and no unrepresented boundary; the exterior region is \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(B)\). Arbitrary topology and collinear or coplanar incidences consistent with these conditions are allowed. Bounded regions have distinct labels \(1,\ldots,r\), with \(r\leq n\), and the exterior has label zero. All vertex coordinates, triangle vertex-index triples and incident labels are explicitly listed. Define \(n\) as their total number of real-coordinate and integer-index entries, including the box. Thus complicated polygon boundaries are charged through their triangulated representation. Any incident region is acceptable for a query on a shared face, edge or vertex, including the exterior on \(\partial B\). The algorithms are finite deterministic programs independent of the input, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each real \(+,-,\times,/\) operation on its domain, comparison, copy or memory access costs one step. Each stored word contains one real or one integer; query-stage integer words have \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged. Floor and digit extraction from reals, size-dependent advice and free geometric oracles are excluded. Storage includes the input retained for queries and temporary query workspace. Preprocessing must halt on every valid input but has no prescribed time or temporary-space bound; only the final stored structure and each query have the stated bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such algorithms, or refute it, with a complete Lean-checked proof. Existence requires constants \(C_s,C_q\) and one pair of uniform algorithms such that every valid subdivision yields a structure of at most \(C_s n\) words and every query is answered correctly within \(C_q\log_2(n+2)\) steps. Refutation must exclude all such pairs in the defined model. Expected performance, a query-distribution promise, linear storage with slower queries, or logarithmic queries with superlinear storage do not establish the positive statement.

cards.title: NP-hardness of three-manifold homeomorphism
cards.formal: Is homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? cards.definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning. The language \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) consists of encodings of satisfiable conjunctions of clauses containing at most three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variable indices and the entire clause list are explicitly encoded in binary; malformed strings are outside the language. A many-one reduction returns one pair, with its entire length and construction time bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). It does not query a homeomorphism oracle or obtain a sequence of adaptive answers. The verifier machinery in the common domain description is not an extra NP-membership assumption on homeomorphism. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, the stated valid-output reduction gives a reduction from every NP language to this promised problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a valid-output reduction exists, or that no such deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists. A positive result must establish the polynomial resource bound, validity of every output manifold and both directions of the satisfiability/homeomorphism equivalence. A negative result must exclude all reductions of this kind. NP-hardness of a related knot, embedding or triangulation-optimization task is insufficient without a reduction to this exact equivalence question. No proof that homeomorphism belongs to NP is required for the positive answer.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s Question 5, attributed there to Burton, asks for NP-hardness of Homeo(3). This card fixes polynomial-time many-one reductions and requires valid triangulated manifolds on every output.

NP-hardness is a lower-bound comparison: any polynomial-time algorithm for homeomorphism would then decide every NP language in polynomial time. It does not assert NP membership, and hence does not by itself assert NP-completeness.
Lackenby establishes hardness relative to graph isomorphism through a many-one reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Graph-isomorphism hardness alone is not the required NP-hardness theorem.

Kuperberg’s elementary-recursive algorithm concerns closed oriented manifolds and provides an upper bound on decision complexity. Such an upper bound is compatible with NP-hardness; decidability and NP-hardness are not mutually exclusive.

The yes/no orientation of the reduction matters. A transformation that sends satisfiable formulas to nonhomeomorphic pairs would instead compare SAT with the complement problem. Likewise, allowing invalid geometric outputs would evade the promised decision task.

A positive answer together with a general NP certificate theorem would make the promised homeomorphism problem NP-complete under valid-output reductions. Combined instead with a coNP certificate theorem, it would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). These consequences explain why the three questions are retained separately.

cards.title: Lower-left anchored rectangle packing constant
cards.formal: Determine the universal lower-left anchored rectangle packing constant \(\alpha\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). For each finite point set \(P\subseteq[0,1)^2\) containing \((0,0)\), let \(A(P)\) be the supremum of the total area of all valid packings of one positive-area axis-aligned rectangle per point, each anchored at that point as its lower-left corner and contained in the unit square. Rectangles must have disjoint interiors. Define \(\alpha=\inf_{P\subseteq[0,1)^2,\;P\text{ finite},\;(0,0)\in P}A(P)\). Area is measured as a fraction of the unit square, so the tolerance is one percentage point of its area.
cards.why: The question asks how much area arbitrary anchors inevitably permit one to occupy. Its mathematical interest comes from the universal guarantee over every finite configuration, including degeneracies, rather than the optimal value of one instance. The half-area conjecture would identify the extremal value, while rigorous estimates of the constant quantify the remaining gap.
cards.status_note: The checked 2021 primary paper and 2023 dissertation leave Freedman’s exact conjecture open and give the interval 0.39 to 0.5 for the associated universal coverage constant. The 2013 proof announcement was explicitly withdrawn. cards.definitions: Write \(p=(x_p,y_p)\). A valid packing chooses real coordinates \(u_p,v_p\) satisfying \(x_p<u_p\le1\) and \(y_p<v_p\le1\) for every \(p\in P\), and uses \(R_p=[x_p,u_p)\times[y_p,v_p)\). For distinct points \(p,q\), the open sets \((x_p,u_p)\times(y_p,v_p)\) and \((x_q,u_q)\times(y_q,v_q)\) must be disjoint; boundaries may touch. Its total area is \(\sum_{p\in P}(u_p-x_p)(v_p-y_p)\). All points are distinct, their number is arbitrary, and coordinates may be any real numbers in the stated domain. Points may share an x-coordinate or y-coordinate; there is no general-position assumption. The origin is mandatory. The other three corners of a rectangle need not belong to \(P\). Every point anchors exactly one positive-area rectangle, and no rotations, other anchor corners, squares-only restriction, or overlaps of positive area are permitted. Valid packings exist for every such finite set, and their areas are bounded by one. Thus \(A(P)\) and \(\alpha\) are well-defined real suprema and infima. No optimum-attaining point set or packing is demanded by the definitions. There is no computational running-time requirement and no rational-coordinate or finite-precision restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha|\le1/100\), with the quantifiers, positivity and boundary conventions above. Equivalently, certify an interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) and take its midpoint. A lower bound \(L\) must hold for every finite allowed point set through its packing supremum; an upper bound \(U\) must bound the infimum over all allowed point sets, allowing a sequence of sets approaching the bound. A value of \(A(P)\) for one selected instance, an uncertified experiment, or only a performance guarantee for a particular algorithm is insufficient. Exact determination is welcome but not required. This numerical benchmark does not claim that a one-percentage-point approximation proves or refutes the exact half-coverage conjecture.

It is not an upper bound of \(0.433\) on the optimum packing constant \(\alpha\), and it does not refute Freedman’s conjecture.

cards.definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm P\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.

cards.definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.

context_blocks.text: A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.

cards.definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. Results allowing the distortion or base-space dimension to grow with |X|, or using exponent 1/p instead of 1/2, do not settle it. No optimal numerical value of C_p is requested.

cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.
